units.t: Persuasion & Rhetoric. Episode two.
In this episode: How to argue well and Body language: fact and fiction.
Part one. How to argue well.
Most arguments are two people defending their egos.
Here's how to have the kind where someone actually learns something.
Getting it right, not winning.
Many of us treat arguments like sport: points scored, opponents defeated.
But if you 'win' while being wrong, you lose the chance to learn.
Writer Julia Galef calls the alternative the scout mindset: the aim is to see things as they are, rather than to defend a position like a soldier defending territory.
In practice, this means going in curious.
Ask yourself: what would I expect to see if I were wrong?
What does this person know that I don't?
The best arguments leave both people understanding more.
Steelman and Rapoport.
A strawman is a weak caricature that is easy to knock down: 'So you think we should just let criminals go free?'
A steelman is the strongest, most charitable form of the argument.
It shows the other person you have heard them, and it tests your own view properly.
A good check is whether they would say, 'Yes, that's exactly what I think.'
Philosopher Daniel Dennett popularised rules he attributed to game theorist Anatol Rapoport.
First, restate their position so fairly they wish they had put it that way.
Second, list points of agreement.
Third, mention what you learned.
Only then criticise.
It changes the temperature of a disagreement.
Ideas and evidence.
In Getting to Yes, 1981, Roger Fisher and William Ury advised separating the people from the problem.
'That plan will blow the budget' targets the idea.
'You always come up with hopeless plans' targets the person, and guarantees defensiveness.
Dismissing an argument because of who made it is the ad hominem fallacy.
Paul Graham's 'hierarchy of disagreement' puts name-calling at the bottom and refuting the central point at the top.
Confidence, repetition and volume prove nothing.
The claimant must support the claim, and not all evidence is equal: an anecdote is weaker than a large study.
Ask 'how do you know?'
of your own beliefs too.
Conceding and updating.
Many people fear that admitting any point weakens their case.
Usually the opposite is true.
Saying 'you're right about the cost' shows fairness and makes your other points more credible.
People also tend to return concessions, as they return favours.
You can give ground on details without abandoning your core view.
Research around 2010 suggested a 'backfire effect', where corrections made people believe more strongly.
Later, larger studies found this is rare: most people shift a little when shown good evidence.
Philip Tetlock found the most accurate forecasters update in small steps.
Think in degrees: 'I'm now 60% sure instead of 90%' is an honest change of mind.
Putting it into practice.
Next time a disagreement starts, try a few habits.
Ask questions before making statements: 'What makes you think that?'
Summarise their view and check you have it right.
Look for the specific point where you actually disagree, as it is often narrower than it first seemed.
Concede what is fair, and keep your tone about the idea.
Also recognise when emotions are too high for good thinking.
'Let's pick this up tomorrow' is not surrender.
Online arguments with strangers rarely change minds; a calm, private conversation with someone who trusts you often does.
If neither of you can name evidence that would change your mind, you may be arguing about values, not facts.
The key idea: The goal of a good argument is to find out what is true, not to beat the other person.
Part two. Body language: fact and fiction.
Crossed arms mean defensive, looking away means lying, and 93% of communication is non-verbal.
Most of that is wrong.
The 93% myth.
You may have heard that only 7% of communication is words, 38% tone of voice and 55% body language.
It comes from experiments by psychologist Albert Mehrabian in 1967.
But his studies were narrow: listeners heard single words and judged whether the speaker liked or disliked someone, when words and tone clashed.
Mehrabian has said his findings don't apply to communication in general.
If 93% of meaning were non-verbal, you could follow a foreign-language film without subtitles.
Body language matters, but words carry most of the content.
Reading signals in context.
Non-verbal signals carry real information.
A slumped posture, a tight jaw or a warm smile can hint at how someone feels.
But a single signal is ambiguous: crossed arms might mean defensiveness, or that the room is cold.
Experts suggest reading clusters of signals and comparing them with the person's normal baseline.
A usually chatty colleague going quiet tells you more than a naturally reserved person being quiet.
Some findings are more solid.
An open posture, facing the person with relaxed shoulders, is seen as warmer.
People who get along often mirror each other, though deliberate copying can backfire if noticed.
Can you spot a liar.
A 2006 review of over 200 studies by Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo found people correctly identify lies and truths only about 54% of the time, barely better than a coin toss.
Police officers do little better.
There is no reliable 'Pinocchio's nose'.
Nervousness and fidgeting show up in anxious truth-tellers too, and practised liars can appear calm.
A 2006 international survey found 'liars avoid eye contact' was the most common lie-detection belief across dozens of countries.
Yet gaze aversion is not a reliable sign of lying, and some liars hold more eye contact.
Looking up and to one side revealing a lie, an idea from neuro-linguistic programming, has not held up in tests.
Focusing on the content of what someone says, such as consistency and checkable detail, works better.
Power posing.
In 2010, researchers Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that holding expansive 'power poses' for two minutes raised testosterone, lowered cortisol and increased risk-taking.
Cuddy's 2012 TED talk on it became one of the most-watched ever.
But a larger 2015 study failed to find the hormone or behaviour effects, and in 2016 Carney said she no longer believed the effects were real.
Researchers still debate whether posture has small effects on how powerful people say they feel.
Standing tall won't hurt you, but it is not a proven hormonal hack.
Culture and eye contact.
In many Western settings, moderate eye contact signals attention, while staring feels aggressive.
One 2016 study found preferred mutual gaze averaged roughly three seconds, with wide individual differences.
In many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, avoiding direct eye contact, particularly with elders, can show respect rather than evasion.
Similar norms exist in parts of Asia.
Misreading this has caused real harm in classrooms, job interviews and courtrooms.
So treat body language as a question, not an answer.
If a friend goes quiet, check in: 'You seem unsure, what's on your mind?'
In high-stakes settings like hiring, be wary of confident claims about reading people.
For your own presence, put the phone away and give genuine attention.
The key idea: The claim that 93% of communication is non-verbal misreads narrow 1960s experiments, and words carry most of the content.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the 'scout mindset' aim for in an argument?
Answer. Seeing things as they are, even if you are wrong.
Question two. Why is the claim that 93% of communication is non-verbal misleading?
Answer. It came from narrow experiments about liking.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
